resources.title: Willow ptarmigan
resources.description: Identify Willow ptarmigan, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Willow ptarmigan (Lagopus lagopus) can be identified as follows: Stocky ptarmigan with a relatively heavy bill; breeding males show rich chestnut head and neck, while winter birds are white with black tails. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Stocky ptarmigan with a relatively heavy bill; breeding males show rich chestnut head and neck, while winter birds are white with black tails.

habitat.text: Willow thickets and low tundra across the North.

resources.title: Rock ptarmigan
resources.description: Identify Rock ptarmigan, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Rock ptarmigan (Lagopus muta) can be identified as follows: Smaller, finer-billed ptarmigan; breeding males have gray upperparts and winter males retain a black eye stripe. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Smaller, finer-billed ptarmigan; breeding males have gray upperparts and winter males retain a black eye stripe.

habitat.text: Rocky Arctic and alpine tundra, generally more exposed than willow ptarmigan habitat.

resources.title: Ring-necked pheasant
resources.description: Identify Ring-necked pheasant, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Ring-necked pheasant (Phasianus colchicus) can be identified as follows: Male has an iridescent green head, red face and very long barred tail; female is mottled buff-brown with a long pointed tail. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: Gray partridge (Perdix perdix) can be identified as follows: Small round gamebird with orange face and throat, barred flanks and a chestnut belly patch that varies by sex and age. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: American woodcock (Scolopax minor) can be identified as follows: Plump, cryptically patterned shorebird with very short legs, large high-set eyes and a long straight bill. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: Wilson's snipe (Gallinago delicata) can be identified as follows: Cryptic marsh bird with a very long straight bill, striped back and a fast zigzag flush. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: Sandhill crane (Antigone canadensis) can be identified as follows: Very large gray bird with long legs, outstretched neck in flight and a red forehead; distinguish carefully from endangered whooping crane. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: Mourning dove (Zenaida macroura) can be identified as follows: Slender tan-gray dove with black wing spots, a small head and a long pointed tail edged in white. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.
